An API is like a helpful messenger that lets two different things talk to each other without them needing to know all the details about how the other works.

Imagine you’re at a coffee shop. You don’t go into the kitchen to make your drink yourself; instead, you tell the barista what you want, and they take care of the rest—grinding the beans, steaming the milk, and handing you the finished cup. The barista’s job is to understand your request, do the work behind the scenes, and give you back exactly what you asked for.

In the same way, an API sits between two programs (or a program and a service). One program says, “I need this piece of information or this action done,” and the API carries that request to the other program, which does the work and then sends back the result. The first program doesn’t have to worry about how the other program stores its data or how it performs its tasks—it just relies on the API to handle the communication smoothly. 

So, an API is simply a set of agreed‑upon ways for one thing to ask another thing for help and get a reply, letting them work together while each stays focused on its own job.
